how: Members call for hands to start, build and defend a shared character drawing.
A starter supplies the initial reference and coordinates and explains why others are needed.
Bare commitments answer recruitment without establishing that every volunteer subsequently placed pixels.
Members judge the labour needed against a design's size and the strength of neighbouring builders.

statement: explaining the canvas to prospective contributors
how: Confused readers require an explanation of pixels, cooldowns and collective pictures after construction is already underway.
Participants choose recognisable characters, smaller variants and designs that could fit neighbouring work.
Members report completed parts and point to new attempts as construction moves between sites.
Reported fandom artwork may be an independent pair's project rather than a single room-directed build.
Reference images, grids and anchor coordinates make the intended sprite and relocation legible to helpers.
Helpers must refresh the current canvas before acting on instructions because stale views can duplicate completed placements.
A request to defer relocation to the starter is a local decision about authority, although later loss of group control limits its reach.
Deference to an initiator does not establish continuing command over builders who later act independently.
Members adapt and revise a shared script, debate adopting it and troubleshoot errors during a restart.
A visitor describes an established shared script as a reason that acknowledging a better border direction does not readily change the collective target.
Completion creates an immediate defence call while other members commit to protecting the threatened drawing.
Clarifying that another figure's arm is friendly construction makes a participant apologise for deleting it and promise to stop.
A visiting memorial defender traces pixel placers through their profiles, a neighbour's surveillance practice rather than local automated placement.
A proposer recognises the neighbour's memorial claim and agrees to look elsewhere.
Participants seek border changes, send a request to a neighbour's pinned discussion and propose coexistence.
A member reports carrying a request into the neighbour's pinned discussion after a visitor directs them there.
Visitors offer relocation help and preservation of neighbouring artwork without documenting delivered assistance.
Separate the offer of repair or relocation labour from assistance actually performed, which these offers do not verify.
A possible alliance is proposed but accepted coalition membership is not established for the room.
Seeking an official spot instantiates the request stage of hosting, while permission and residence remain unresolved.
Erasure prompts proposals for a less contested location and a smaller design.
Relocation can be precautionary before an approaching work arrives or normative when builders recognise a neighbour's protected claim.
A restart reopens the choice between character designs instead of resuming an unchanged shared mark.
Restarting also reopens anchor-coordinate decisions, creating a local return from relocation to shared placement instructions.
Loss of operational group control does not establish a dispute over anyone's right to commit the room to a treaty.
Fandom lore is carried into the organising thread as an Old Bird joke that another participant does not recognise.
Only the lore-specific part of the joking theme supports fandom identity, while generic sand and gravel riffs belong with April Fools play.
National entitlement and flag claims voiced by visiting builders must not be attributed to the host fandom as its own national identity.
The recorded conflict identifies a canvas neighbour and claims first arrival without establishing a quarrel inherited from before the event.
Lore and canvas rivalry both occur, but the record does not show a prior tie selecting the attacked neighbour.
Fake game news and image pranks invite recognition, complaints, praise and further playful replies alongside canvas organising.
A fake game's appeal leads to recommending an existing substitute and an intention to play it, rather than retaining a temporary prank restyle.
Members dispute the canvas's worth through competing expectations of lasting internet history and rapid forgetting.
Completion is celebrated before the event ends, with separate credit for a finished drawing the initiator did not help complete.
Members record loss, mourn Samus, mark the end and take consolation in brief time-lapse visibility.
A post-event reply proposes requesting cleanup of a shared canvas copy to recover Samus, without evidence of execution.
A cleanup suggestion does not establish a successor canvas, lasting organisation or another adopted use for the temporary effort.
War language and a proposal to occupy apparent stripes show contemplated encroachment, without proving a coordinated raid.
Participants carry the canvas conflict into blame of the blue corner after the event ends.
A starter's call receives a joining response that explicitly describes work already completed and how the build is proceeding.
A member who has already begun a solo drawing explicitly asks others to make its completion possible.
One announcement couples a completed drawing directly to a call to defend it.
A dispute over space for existing pixel art develops into a directed request on the neighbour's pinned discussion.
Restraint can follow recognising a meaningful memorial claim without a previously settled border or treaty.
Perceived competitive necessity justifies script adoption during rebuilding, while the record cannot establish a maintenance system or successful placement.
Announcements that the drawing is complete supply direct evidence of celebrating achievement rather than merely planning it.
The celebrant subsequently qualifies the screenshot's age and records total loss in the same thread.
Recording loss leads to a cleanup suggestion, but no demonstrated transition into a lasting successor effort follows within the record.
Perceived insufficient hands can concentrate effort on the existing drawing, and invested labour can delay a restart instead of producing immediate relocation.
A posted reference remains revisable when participants discover errors, so its circulation alone does not establish agreement on the final design.
Bare joining replies instantiate the proposed call-and-answer form, without testing whether silent placers felt an obligation to answer.
Offers of help do not show that maintenance shortages caused a request or that another room subsequently delivered repair labour.
Negotiation and later assistance offers coexist without an explicit link showing that a border deal opened a reciprocal exchange.
A recruitment thread later contains a war proposal and explicit assent, supporting a local sequence without proving recruitment caused aggression.
An encroachment proposal receives flag-identification objections, followed by explicit withdrawal from that flag.
A proposal to occupy apparent stripes is answered by an invitation to negotiate before placing on the identified flag.
A war proposal receives a visiting builder's warning that they remain ready to battle and should not be interfered with.
A hoped-for alliance and an intended host application do not establish upkeep leading to actual coalition membership.
Arguments over the canvas's worth and a proposal-withdrawal removal request do not establish a flood of calls causing host moderation.
A neighbour's request exposes dispersed operational control but no explicit dispute over who may conclude an agreement for the room.
A celebratory report or maintenance call does not verify final survival, especially when the screenshot predates the post or placement has ended.
